feature.headline: Everybody Drafted, Nobody Escaped
feature.standfirst: Fifteen rounds, twelve rosters, four tight ends nobody can start, and a kicker taken before half the league had a second quarterback.

sections.heading: Bree's Badass Boys Went Kicker Shopping Twice
body: Round seven, with the board still stocked, Bree took Eddy Pineiro. That is a kicker in the seventh, in a format where the OP slot eats a second quarterback every week. Then, in the eleventh, Bree went back and took Harrison Butker. Two kickers, one kicker slot, five bench spots total, and now one of them is permanently occupied by a man who will never appear in the lineup unless the other one gets hurt on a Saturday.

The rest of the roster tells the same story. A.J. Brown and Davante Adams and George Kittle are real players, and then the back half turns into a scratch-off card: Mike Washington Jr., Camden Brown, and Kirk Cousins in the fifteenth, a quarterback whose last full act as a starter was being benched for a rookie in Atlanta. Bree built a starting nine and then spent the bench on hobbies.

sections.heading: Justin Stacked Tight Ends In A One-TE League
body: Substation Superstars took Brock Bowers in the fourth, and that is fine, that is a real player. Then Sam LaPorta in the ninth. Then Mark Andrews in the eleventh. That is three tight ends for one tight end slot, so every Sunday two of them sit on a bench that only holds five and is now sixty percent tight end. The roster cap says three. Justin found the cap and shook its hand.

The finish was the flourish. Deshaun Watson, taken in the fifteenth, a quarterback who has thrown for a full season's worth of nothing since arriving in Cleveland and who has spent more time on the injury report than the depth chart. Justin already had Trevor Lawrence. He needed a second starter. He took the one that comes with the longest paper trail in the league.

sections.heading: Tyler Collected Quarterbacks Like Baseball Cards
body: Tyler's Talented Team opened with Bijan Robinson and Amon-Ra St. Brown and then, apparently overcome, took five quarterbacks. Jared Goff, Sam Darnold, Bryce Young, Aaron Rodgers, and the roster cap is four, so somebody in there is a trade chip or a coat rack. Superflex starts two. Tyler drafted a quarterback room, a quarterback waiting room, and a quarterback overflow area.

Darnold in the fifth is the one that hurts, a player whose career has been a series of teams deciding he was the answer and then quietly deciding he wasn't. Rodgers in the tenth is forty-one years old and on his third organization. Then Travis Kelce in the eleventh, which is genuinely the best available tight end on the board, sandwiched between quarterbacks nobody can start. Tyler found the value and buried it.

sections.heading: Jesse Went All-In On Injury Reports
body: Mr. Anderson took Josh Allen first overall and then spent the middle rounds assembling the most fragile receiver corps in the league. George Pickens, Chris Olave, Christian Watson, DK Metcalf. Olave has been through the concussion protocol enough times that the protocol knows his name. Watson tore his ACL in the last game of last season. That is a wide receiver group that requires a group chat with a physical therapist.

The backfield went the same direction, four deep with Chase Brown, David Montgomery, Blake Corum, Chuba Hubbard, and Zach Charbonnet, none of whom get the ball alone. Then Caleb Williams in the second as the OP starter, a quarterback whose rookie year was mostly running for his life. Jesse built a roster that will be exciting for about nine weeks.

sections.heading: Nobody Told Chenell About The Second Quarterback
body: Da Reigning Champ actually did the superflex math early, Lamar Jackson in the first and Dak Prescott in the third, and then went back to the well in the thirteenth for Tua Tagovailoa. That is a quarterback whose availability has been the central question of his career and who is more discussed than played. Three quarterbacks is defensible. That third one is a decision.

The larger issue is Harrison Mevis in the ninth. A kicker, in the ninth round, with Jordan Addison and Kyle Monangai and a hundred other useful bodies still sitting there. The bench math in this league is brutal, five spots, and Chenell spent one of the good rounds on the man who kicks the extra points. The Chargers D/ST at the very end at least came in the round where defenses belong.

sections.heading: Colin Bet The Season On Rookie Quarterbacks
body: 4th and Inshes went Bo Nix in the third and Tyler Shough in the sixth, which is a superflex starting pair built entirely out of quarterbacks with fewer than two full seasons of NFL starts between them. Shough is a rookie who spent seven years in college football, which isn't a joke, that is the actual biography. Then Jacoby Brissett in the eleventh as the emergency parachute, a man whose entire career has been being the emergency parachute.

The rest is sturdy. Puka Nacua, James Cook III, Nico Collins, Zay Flowers, TreVeyon Henderson. Travis Hunter in the twelfth is the fun swing, a two-way player whose usage plan changes depending on which coach is being interviewed. Colin built a very good non-quarterback team in a league where two quarterbacks start every week.

sections.heading: Jay Doubled Up On Defenses Instead
body: Jay's Team took Jahmyr Gibbs first, which was correct, and Breece Hall and Kyren Williams after that, which built the deepest backfield in the room. Then, in rounds eleven and twelve, Jay took the Broncos D/ST and the Rams D/ST back to back. Two defenses. One D/ST slot. Two of the five bench spots gone before a single bye week arrives.

The quarterback plan is Justin Herbert and Malik Willis, and Willis is a backup who exists to hand the ball off when Jordan Love isn't available. That is the OP slot. Fernando Mendoza went in the fourteenth as the deep swing. Jay assembled a running back factory and then staffed the most important position in the format with a fire extinguisher.

teams.verdict: Two Quarterbacks, Nine Running Backs, One Prayer
teams.teaser: Josh Allen and Caleb Williams anchor a roster that then spent the rest of the draft collecting running backs like bottle caps.
body: Josh Allen at the top of a superflex board is the least controversial thing anyone did all night. Then the wheel came back and Caleb Williams arrived as QB2, which is a bet that a young passer figures it out on your schedule rather than his own. That is the whole quarterback room. Two arms in a format that starts twenty-four, and no third body if either one gets a week off.

Where the roster actually went sideways is the backfield. Chase Brown, David Montgomery, Jadarian Price, Blake Corum, Chuba Hubbard, Zach Charbonnet, six running backs plus the flex ambitions of a receiver corps built on George Pickens, Chris Olave, Christian Watson and DK Metcalf. That is a lot of guys competing for two starting slots and one flex, on five bench spots. Corum and Charbonnet in particular are handcuff-shaped: useful the week something bad happens somewhere else, dead weight the other sixteen. Meanwhile Dalton Kincaid is the lone tight end, which at least means nobody is stranded.

The receivers share a theme worth noticing: Pickens, Olave, Watson and Metcalf are all players whose ceiling arrives attached to a health note or a target-share argument. Pair them with a quarterback room of two and the margin for a bad Sunday is thin. Evan McPherson closed things out, and taking a kicker with the final pick of the draft is the one universally correct decision available. The rest of this team is a running back convention that forgot to book a second room.

teams.teaser: Justin Jefferson and Malik Nabers headline a receiver room so deep that Doug forgot the bench only holds five.
body: Jayden Daniels and Baker Mayfield is a real superflex pairing, and Ashton Jeanty and Bucky Irving is a real backfield. If the draft had ended after six rounds this would read like a contender. It didn't end after six rounds.

What followed was a receiver hoarding spree. Justin Jefferson, Malik Nabers, Parker Washington, Josh Downs, Jayden Reed, Chris Godwin Jr. and Deebo Samuel Sr. is seven wideouts for two starting spots and a flex that a running back also wants. Godwin and Reed both arrive with their own history of missed time, Downs and Washington are slot bodies fighting the same target trees, and Deebo is a player whose value depends entirely on a coaching staff scheming him touches. Five bench spots. Seven receivers. The math doesn't resolve, and somebody good is getting cut in week two so a bye-week quarterback can exist.

Brandon Aubrey in the ninth is the loudest decision on the sheet. He is the best kicker alive and he is still a kicker, taken six rounds before anyone needed to think about the position, in a league where the last pick of the draft handles it fine. Kyle Pitts Sr. is the tight end, which is the eternal wager on a fourth-year breakout that keeps being scheduled and never arriving. The talent at the top is genuine. The back half is a receiver room with a hoarding problem and a kicker who thinks he is a wide receiver.

teams.verdict: Three Quarterbacks, All Of Them Nervous
teams.teaser: De'Von Achane and Saquon Barkley are a dream backfield attached to a quarterback room held together with Geno Smith.
body: De'Von Achane and Saquon Barkley back to back is the best two-pick sequence in the room, and Tyler Warren at tight end fills the one slot that ruins seasons. Ladd McConkey and Garrett Wilson give the receiver corps a spine. This is a well-built offense.

The quarterbacks are the argument. Matthew Stafford is the anchor, a veteran whose back has been a recurring preseason storyline for years now. Jordan Love is the upside swing. Geno Smith is the third, which is admirable roster hygiene in superflex, because three arms means a bye week is a shrug instead of a crisis. But none of the three is the kind of passer who wins a week by himself, and in a six-point-passing-touchdown format that is where the points live. Keshia built a running back team and then had to start two quarterbacks anyway.

The back half doubles down on the backfield: Jaylen Warren, Tony Pollard and Aaron Jones Sr. behind Achane and Barkley is five running backs for two slots, and Jones in particular is a veteran whose seasons keep getting interrupted. Xavier Worthy and Khalil Shakir round out the receivers with a pair of guys whose production swings entirely on whether their quarterback looks their way. Trey Smack with the second-to-last pick is a fine place to find a kicker. The Steelers defense is the Steelers defense. The core is excellent, the arms are a group project, and the bench is running backs stacked on running backs.

teams.verdict: The Champ Drafted Four Quarterbacks, Somehow
teams.teaser: Lamar Jackson leads a roster with a quarterback problem, a wide receiver problem, and a kicker taken in the ninth.
body: Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry is a title-defense opening. Dak Prescott as the second starter is a genuine superflex answer, and Javonte Williams behind Henry gives the backfield two real bodies. Through four rounds the reigning champion looked like the reigning champion.

Then the ninth round happened. Harrison Mevis is a kicker, taken with six rounds still to play, in a format where kickers are the last thing anybody should think about. Six picks later came Tua Tagovailoa as a fourth quarterback, and Tua's story is the most fraught in the sport, a player whose career has been repeatedly interrupted by head injuries and whose availability nobody can promise. Four arms on a fifteen-man roster, one of them a lottery ticket that nobody enjoys buying, all while five bench spots have to also hold receivers.

The receiver room is where the season likely turns. DeVonta Smith, DJ Moore, Jordan Addison, Quentin Johnston and KC Concepcion is a collection of second and third options on offenses that have better first options. Nobody there commands a target share. Isaiah Likely is the tight end, a player who has spent his whole career being the more exciting half of a two-tight-end room without ever getting the snaps to prove it. Rhamondre Stevenson and Kyle Monangai add backfield depth behind a Henry who has been carrying the ball professionally for a very long time. The top is a champion's roster. The bottom is a kicker in the ninth.

teams.verdict: Two Kickers, One Great Draft Gone Wrong
teams.teaser: Jalen Hurts and A.J. Brown open beautifully, then the roster picks up a kicker in the seventh and another in the eleventh.
body: Jalen Hurts, A.J. Brown, Kenneth Walker III, C.J. Stroud, Davante Adams, George Kittle. Six rounds, six real players, a genuine superflex quarterback pairing and the best blocking tight end in football who also happens to catch things. Adams is deep into his thirties and Kittle's body has an injury history you could read as a novel, but this is a starting lineup that wins weeks.

Round seven is where it stops. Eddy Pineiro is a kicker, taken while actual starters were still on the board, and then Harrison Butker arrives in the eleventh as the second kicker on a fifteen-man roster. The cap is two, so this is legal. It is also two roster spots spent on a position where one guy who kicks is functionally the same as any other guy who kicks, on a team that has five bench spots total. That is forty percent of the bench dedicated to the game's most replaceable job.

The rest of the back half is swing after swing. Mike Washington Jr., Camden Brown, Brian Robinson Jr., Tyjae Spears, deep names hoping for a depth chart to open up. Kirk Cousins closes the draft as a third quarterback, and Cousins right now is a veteran holding a clipboard behind somebody younger, which is a strange thing to want on purpose. The Ravens defense in the eighth was early for a unit, but at least a defense plays every week. The top six here belong in the playoff conversation. Rounds seven through fifteen belong in a cautionary tale about the special teams budget.

teams.verdict: Elite Running Backs, Malik Willis As QB2
teams.teaser: Jahmyr Gibbs and Breece Hall headline a loaded backfield, and then the superflex slot gets handed to Malik Willis.
body: Jahmyr Gibbs first overall, CeeDee Lamb, then Kyren Williams and Breece Hall. That is a backfield nobody else in this league can match, three genuine every-week starters plus Rico Dowdle later as a fourth. In half PPR that is points every Sunday. The problem is that only two of them can start, and the flex is one seat.

Justin Herbert is a fine QB1. Malik Willis is the second quarterback, and Willis has spent his career as an emergency option, a backup who was genuinely good in relief and then handed the job back the moment the starter was healthy. In a format that starts two quarterbacks with six-point passing touchdowns, that is a hole in the lineup card every single week, not a bye-week problem. Fernando Mendoza arrives in the fourteenth as the third arm, which is a rookie flier rather than a solution.

The bench is where the resources went instead. Two defenses, Broncos and Rams, taken in back-to-back rounds. Both play the same Sunday, both occupy a spot, and only one can be in the lineup. Add Dallas Goedert at tight end, a player whose seasons come with a missed-games line item, plus Tee Higgins and Michael Pittman Jr. as the receiver support behind Lamb, and the five bench slots are already full before anyone considers what happens when Herbert has a bye. Jay built the best set of running backs in the room and then left the most valuable position in the format to a guy whose job is to hold the ball until somebody else arrives.

teams.verdict: Five Quarterbacks, And Rodgers Is One
teams.teaser: Bijan Robinson and Amon-Ra St. Brown are elite, and then the roster collects quarterbacks like a man who cannot pick a favorite.
body: Bijan Robinson and Amon-Ra St. Brown is as clean a start as this draft offered. Drake London next makes the receiver room genuinely dangerous. Jared Goff is a perfectly good superflex anchor, and D'Andre Swift and Bhayshul Tuten give the backfield actual bodies behind Bijan. Through seven rounds this is a very good football team.

Then the quarterback collecting began. Sam Darnold in the fifth, Bryce Young in the ninth, Aaron Rodgers in the tenth. With Goff that is four arms, the roster maximum, on a fifteen-man team with five bench spots. Two of them start. The other two sit, and one of them is Rodgers, who is forty-one and playing for his third team in four years, a quarterback whose every season now comes with a documentary crew and a farewell tour that keeps getting extended. Bryce Young is the other, a former first overall pick who has already been benched once for a career backup. Between them, that is two bench slots spent on stories rather than points.

What got squeezed out is depth everywhere else. Marvin Harrison Jr. and Stefon Diggs are the receiver support, Diggs coming off a serious knee injury and now on his third team in three years. Travis Kelce is the tight end, and Kelce at thirty-six is a player whose route tree has visibly shortened. Rachaad White is the fourth running back. Tyler Loop and the Jets defense close it out, which is exactly where those belong. Tyler had the makings of the best roster here and spent a third of it on quarterbacks he cannot start.

teams.verdict: Puka Nacua, Then A Rookie Quarterback Committee
teams.teaser: Puka Nacua and Nico Collins are real, and the quarterback room is Bo Nix, Tyler Shough and a career backup.
body: Puka Nacua, James Cook III, Nico Collins, Zay Flowers. That is a receiving corps with two genuine alphas and a backfield with a workhorse. Harold Fannin Jr. at tight end is a rookie bet but a cheap one, and TreVeyon Henderson gives the backfield explosive upside behind Cook. The skill positions are in good shape.

The quarterbacks aren't. Bo Nix is the starter, Tyler Shough is the second arm, and Shough is a quarterback who spent seven years in college football and arrives as a rookie older than several established starters. Jacoby Brissett is the third, a professional caretaker whose entire career has been keeping a seat warm. In a superflex with six-point passing touchdowns, that trio is asking a lot of Nix and hoping the rest sorts itself out. Three quarterbacks means the byes are covered. It does not mean the points are.

The back half went shopping for names with stories attached. J.K. Dobbins has an injury history that has defined his career. Mike Evans is thirty-two and still producing, which is impressive and also finite. Travis Hunter is the two-way experiment nobody has ever run at this level, and fantasy has no idea what to do with a receiver who also plays corner. RJ Harvey adds a fourth running back. Ka'imi Fairbairn and the Jaguars defense arrive at the correct time, which is late. Colin drafted good football players and then handed the most valuable position in the format to a committee that would look conservative in a single-quarterback league.

teams.verdict: Four Elite Picks, Then A Lottery Habit
teams.teaser: McCaffrey, Chase, Purdy and Mahomes is a genuine core, and then the roster starts buying scratch tickets.
body: Christian McCaffrey and Ja'Marr Chase to open, then Brock Purdy and Patrick Mahomes as the quarterback pairing. That is the most balanced top four in the room. Travis Etienne Jr. and Jaylen Waddle add real production, and Colston Loveland is a reasonable bet at a position where reasonable bets are all that exist. McCaffrey turns thirty this season and has spent recent years fighting his own soft tissue, but when he plays he is still the best version of the job.

From the eighth round on, this becomes a stack of deep-league fliers. MarShawn Lloyd is a running back whose rookie year was almost entirely spent unavailable. Jordyn Tyson and Tyler Allgeier are depth-chart-dependent names. Alec Pierce is a deep threat whose weekly output looks like a heart monitor. Brian Thomas Jr. and Jordan Mason are the most defensible of the bunch. None of it is offensive on its own. Collectively it is five bench spots holding maybes when the top of the roster deserved insurance.

The bigger structural issue is quarterback. Purdy and Mahomes both start every week, which is correct, and there is no third arm anywhere on the sheet. Two quarterbacks in a format that starts two means the first bye week is a scramble on the wire against eleven teams with the same idea. Cairo Santos and the Packers defense close things out in the right rounds. James assembled a genuinely strong starting lineup and then spent the entire back half buying lottery tickets instead of a spare tire.

teams.verdict: Three Tight Ends, One Tight End Slot
teams.teaser: Jonathan Taylor anchors a strong roster that then drafted Brock Bowers, Sam LaPorta and Mark Andrews for one starting spot.
body: Jonathan Taylor first, Trevor Lawrence second, Rashee Rice third. Solid. Emeka Egbuka, Rome Odunze and Courtland Sutton give the receiver room three legitimate contributors, and Josh Jacobs is a genuine workhorse in the backfield. This roster has real weeks in it.

And then there are the tight ends. Brock Bowers in the fourth is defensible, because he is the best at the position. Sam LaPorta in the ninth is a fine player. Mark Andrews in the eleventh is a fine player. There is one tight end slot. Andrews is also on the wrong side of thirty at a position that ages badly and coming off a season where he split work with a younger teammate. That is the roster maximum of three tight ends, two of whom sit every Sunday, on a bench that holds five. Two bench spots gone to a position that pays out once a week.

The defenses compound it. Texans in the twelfth, Browns in the thirteenth, both occupying space on the same bench. That is four of five bench slots committed to players who cannot all play. Deshaun Watson closes the draft as the third quarterback, a passer who hasn't looked like himself since the trade and whose last two seasons ended with a torn Achilles. The starting lineup here is competitive. The bench is a museum of players who are excellent at jobs this team already filled.

teams.verdict: Drake Maye's Team, Jaxson Dart's Problem
teams.teaser: A young quarterback room and a deep receiver group, undermined by two running backs who cannot be counted on.
body: Drake Maye is a genuine superflex QB1 and Jeremiyah Love in the third is a real swing at a backfield. Trey McBride at tight end is the best non-Bowers answer available at the position, and Terry McLaurin, Tetairoa McMillan and Jameson Williams give the receiver room three different ways to score. Daniel Jones in the eighth is the third quarterback, which is the correct amount of insurance.

Jaxson Dart as the second starter is the load-bearing risk. He is a rookie being asked to produce six-point passing touchdowns every week from the moment the season starts, and rookie quarterbacks are famously a smooth, linear experience. Mike drafted two quarterbacks in the first thirty-five picks and both of them are still figuring out professional football. That could look brilliant in November. It could also look like two lineup slots producing single digits.

The backfield is the actual crisis. Behind Love there is Jonathon Brooks, a running back whose young career has been defined by knee injuries and rehab timelines, and Kaleb Johnson in the fifteenth. That is it. Two running backs and a rookie who has spent more time in a training room than a huddle, in a league that starts two plus a flex. Jake Ferguson gives the roster a second tight end for one slot, and Cameron Dicker and the Lions defense arrive appropriately late. The receiver room is deep enough to carry a flex. The backfield is one bad Sunday from a waiver-wire emergency.

teams.verdict: Four Quarterbacks, Three Of Them Homework
teams.teaser: Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Joe Burrow open strong, then the roster spends the back half on quarterbacks who may never start.
body: Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Joe Burrow is an excellent two-round start, and Omarion Hampton, Quinshon Judkins and Cam Skattebo behind them build a young, physical backfield with actual volume. Kyler Murray is a real second starter. Tucker Kraft is a sensible tight end. The bones here are good, and the running back room in particular could be the surprise of the season.

Then the quarterback accumulation. Cam Ward in the ninth is the third arm, a rookie taken first overall by a rebuilding team. Drew Allar in the fifteenth is the fourth, and Allar is a college quarterback. That is the roster maximum at the position, two of them unable to help this season in any meaningful way, on a bench that holds five. Burrow's own recent history is a season cut short by injury, so wanting depth is understandable. Wanting four is a collection.

The receiver room paid for it. Behind Smith-Njigba there is Luther Burden III, Carnell Tate and De'Zhaun Stribling, rookies and deep-roster names all hoping a depth chart opens up. Two starting receiver spots plus a flex, and only one of them has a name anybody would want to start in week one. Kenny Gainwell adds a fourth running back. Cam Little and the Patriots defense land in exactly the right rounds, which is the cleanest thing on the sheet. Evan built a strong backfield, a top receiver, and then spent the endgame drafting quarterbacks he will spend the season reading about instead of starting.
